prompt: What does the term "organic chemistry" literally mean?

choices.text: The chemistry of life
The chemistry of natural, pesticide-free products
choices.why: That is the everyday, grocery-store sense of "organic". In chemistry the name comes from the chemistry of living things.

choices.text: The chemistry of metals
choices.why: Metals were traditionally grouped with non-living things, the historical territory of inorganic chemistry, not organic chemistry.

choices.text: The chemistry of minerals
choices.why: Minerals seemed to be made of elements other than carbon, so historically they belonged to inorganic chemistry.

explanation: "Organic chemistry" literally means the chemistry of life. It became the study of carbon-based molecules because the first molecules isolated from living organisms contained carbon.

prompt: Why did organic chemistry come to be the study of carbon-based molecules?

choices.text: The first molecules isolated from living organisms contained carbon
Carbon was the first element ever discovered
choices.why: The name has to do with the molecules of living things, not with the order in which elements were discovered.

choices.text: Carbon compounds can't conduct electricity, unlike metals
choices.why: Some carbon-based materials do conduct electricity, which is one reason inorganic chemists study them. It isn't why organic chemistry is about carbon.

choices.text: Carbon is the only element found in living things
choices.why: The definition came from which molecules were isolated first, not from carbon being the only element in living things.

explanation: The first molecules isolated from living organisms contained carbon, while minerals and other non-living things seemed to be made of other elements. So organic chemistry, the chemistry of life, became the study of carbon-based molecules.

prompt: For some time in history, what did scientists believe was the chemical difference between living and non-living things?

choices.text: Carbon
Metals
choices.why: Metals weren't the believed dividing line. The belief was that living things were carbon-based, while minerals and other non-living things were made of other elements.

choices.text: Water
choices.why: The belief was about carbon: the first molecules from living organisms contained it, and minerals seemed not to.

choices.text: Electrical conductivity
choices.why: Conductivity comes up as a reason the modern field includes some carbon molecules, not as the historic dividing line between living and non-living.

explanation: Molecules isolated from living organisms contained carbon, while minerals and other non-living things seemed to be made of other elements, so for some time scientists believed carbon was the chemical difference between living and non-living things.

choices.text: The chemistry of non-living things, made of non-carbon molecules and ions
The chemistry of living things that contain metals
choices.why: Historically, living things belonged to organic chemistry. Inorganic chemistry was the chemistry of non-living things, such as minerals.

choices.text: The chemistry of carbon compounds made in a laboratory
choices.why: The historical dividing line was carbon itself: inorganic meant non-carbon molecules and ions, not carbon compounds of any origin.

choices.text: The chemistry of gases, such as air
choices.why: The historical meaning covered non-living things in general, such as minerals, not one particular phase of matter.

explanation: If organic molecules were the molecules of life, inorganic chemistry historically meant the chemistry of non-living things, and these were non-carbon molecules and ions.

prompt: What is a generally accepted definition of inorganic chemistry today?

choices.text: The study of non-carbon molecules: all the elements on the periodic table except carbon
The study of metals and nothing else
choices.why: The accepted definition covers every element except carbon, the nonmetals included, not just the metals.

choices.text: The chemistry of non-living things
choices.why: That is the historical meaning. Today's generally accepted definition is about elements: everything on the periodic table except carbon.

choices.text: The study of compounds in which metals are bonded to carbon
choices.why: Those are organometallic compounds. Inorganic chemistry includes them, but they are only one part of the field, not its definition.

explanation: A generally accepted definition of inorganic chemistry is the study of non-carbon molecules, or all the elements on the periodic table except carbon. It isn't completely correct, because the field also reaches into some carbon compounds.

prompt: Why is "the study of every element except carbon" not a completely correct definition of inorganic chemistry?

choices.text: The field also includes organometallic compounds and some carbon-based molecules with metal-like properties
Some elements other than carbon belong only to organic chemistry
choices.why: The problem isn't that other elements are missing from inorganic chemistry. It's that inorganic chemistry also reaches into carbon compounds.

choices.text: Inorganic chemistry really studies only a handful of elements
choices.why: The opposite: the field is very broad, practically limitless.

choices.text: Organic chemists no longer study carbon compounds
choices.why: Organic chemistry is still the study of carbon-based molecules. The definition fails because inorganic chemistry covers some carbon compounds too.

explanation: Inorganic chemistry also includes organometallic compounds and some carbon-based molecules with properties familiar from metals, such as conducting electricity. So "everything except carbon" leaves out part of the field.

prompt: Inorganic chemists study some carbon-based molecules because they have a property familiar from metals. Which property does the section give as its example?

choices.text: Conducting electricity
Being isolated from living organisms
choices.why: Coming from living things is what historically made molecules organic, not a property familiar from metals.

choices.text: Containing hydrogen
choices.why: The section's example is conduction of electricity, a property familiar from metals. Containing hydrogen isn't a metal-like property.

choices.text: Dissolving in water
choices.why: The section's example is conduction of electricity, a property familiar from metals, not solubility.

explanation: Inorganic chemistry includes the study of some carbon-based molecules with properties familiar from metals, like conduction of electricity.

prompt: A compound has a metal atom bonded to carbon. Does it belong to the field of inorganic chemistry?

choices.text: Yes: inorganic chemistry includes organometallic compounds, even though they contain carbon
No: any compound that contains carbon belongs to organic chemistry
choices.why: That follows the "everything except carbon" definition, which isn't completely correct: the field also includes organometallic compounds.

choices.text: No: inorganic chemistry studies only pure elements
choices.why: Inorganic chemistry studies molecules and ions, not only pure elements.

choices.text: Only if the compound occurs naturally in a mineral
choices.why: There's no such condition. Organometallic compounds belong to inorganic chemistry whether they come from minerals, laboratories, or living things.

explanation: The field of inorganic chemistry includes organometallic compounds, which is one reason "all the elements except carbon" isn't a completely correct definition.

prompt: How does the section describe the scope of inorganic chemistry?

choices.text: Very broad, practically limitless
A narrow specialty focused on minerals
choices.why: Minerals were part of its historical meaning, but the modern field covers every element except carbon and some carbon compounds too.

choices.text: Smaller than organic chemistry, because it leaves out carbon
choices.why: Leaving out carbon still leaves every other element, and the field reaches into some carbon compounds as well.

choices.text: Limited to metals and their ores
choices.why: The field covers all the elements except carbon, the nonmetals included, plus organometallic compounds and some carbon-based materials.

explanation: Because inorganic chemistry covers all the elements except carbon, and also organometallic compounds and some carbon-based molecules, the section calls the field very broad, and practically limitless.

prompt: What does the section suggest as a great way to understand the breadth of inorganic chemistry?

choices.text: Look at the titles and abstracts in recent issues of the journal Inorganic Chemistry
Count the elements on the periodic table other than carbon
choices.why: The definition already says "all the elements except carbon". The section's suggestion is to see the range of research actually being published.

choices.text: Read about the history of alchemy
choices.why: History explains where the field came from, not how broad it is today. The section points to recent articles in the journal Inorganic Chemistry.

explanation: The section suggests looking at the abstracts in the latest issues of the journal Inorganic Chemistry, or its most-read articles, to see how broad the field is.

prompt: A student skims a recent issue of Inorganic Chemistry and notices that many of the sub-fields they find also involve another discipline. What does that show?

choices.text: That's expected: many other fields overlap with inorganic chemistry, so many sub-fields are interdisciplinary
Those articles were published in the wrong journal
choices.why: Overlap is normal. Inorganic chemistry has something for almost everyone because many other fields overlap with it.

choices.text: Inorganic chemistry is really a branch of organic chemistry
choices.why: Overlapping with other fields doesn't make inorganic chemistry a branch of any one of them. It shows how broad the field is.

choices.text: Inorganic chemistry has exactly four sub-fields
choices.why: The practice asks for at least 4 sub-fields, and there are many correct answers. The field is very broad.

explanation: The section's practice notes there are many correct answers: inorganic chemistry is very broad, many other fields overlap with it, and some of its sub-fields are interdisciplinary fields between inorganic chemistry and another discipline.

prompt: Which statement about the words "organic" and "inorganic" is correct?

choices.text: The names come from science history, and the modern understanding of the two fields doesn't match those historical meanings
Modern organic chemistry studies only molecules isolated from living organisms
choices.why: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon-based molecules, wherever they come from, not only molecules taken from living things.

choices.text: Modern inorganic chemistry still means the chemistry of non-living things
choices.why: That is the historical meaning. The modern understanding isn't consistent with it.

choices.text: The historical meanings were replaced by an exact, agreed dividing line
choices.why: There is no exact line: even the generally accepted definition, everything except carbon, isn't completely correct.

explanation: The names organic and inorganic come from science history, when organic meant the chemistry of life and inorganic the chemistry of non-living things. The modern understanding of the two fields is not consistent with these historical meanings.
